transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Um, I guess I'm just here because... well, I've been spending a little too much time double-checking things lately. It's probably nothing major, just, you know, wanting to be thorough. I work as an engineer, so being precise is kind of part of the job, right? 

But, um, it's gotten to the point where I'm losing a few hours a day just... rechecking. Things like my dressing supplies, the door locks, file dimensions at work, revision notes... I just have this routine I feel like I need to go through. I don't really feel, I don't know, allowed to move on to the next thing until I've done it enough times that the anxiety kind of settles down. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining that okay.
Can you tell me more about the thoughts you have when you're rechecking these things? Are they thoughts that you don't really want to have, or do they feel intrusive in any way?

Um, yeah, I guess... I mean, I'm sure everyone worries a little bit about doing a good job, right? But... well, it does feel a bit like they just pop up when I don't want them to. It sounds kind of silly to say out loud, but even after I absolutely *know* I’ve cleaned a wound area perfectly, or I've thoroughly reviewed a CAD file at work, this... this thought just keeps cutting in. 

It's always telling me that I missed one tiny thing, and because of that, it’s going to turn into a bad infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. And no matter how much logic I try to use, I just can’t seem to reason it away. I really try to, but it just sticks there. 

Does that answer your question? I hope I'm not making it sound weirder than it actually is. Is that what you mean by intrusive?

When you feel that anxiety about possibly missing something, do you feel like you have to perform these checking rituals in a specific way or for a certain amount of time in order to feel reassured or to prevent something bad from happening?

Um, yes, exactly. I guess I kind of mentioned it before, but... yeah, I do have a specific way I have to do it. It's not like I'm doing anything crazy, I promise. It's just... well, like I said, I'm losing hours to it. 

When I check my dressing supplies, or the locks, or my file dimensions and revision notes at work, I have to go through this exact same routine. I don't really feel... allowed, I guess, to move on until I've done it enough times. Like, I have to repeat the steps until that heavy, anxious feeling finally drops enough for me to breathe. 

I know it sounds like a lot of time to waste, and I probably shouldn't be letting it take up so many hours, but it's the only way I can feel sure that nothing bad is going to happen. I just want to be safe and do a good job. Is that... is that a normal reaction to stress? I really hope I'm giving you the right kind of information.
Do these checking routines cause you any significant distress or interfere with your daily life, work, or relationships?

Um, well... I wouldn't say it's, like, ruining my life or anything. I'm still functioning, you know? But... I guess it is causing some issues. It's embarrassing to admit, but... my project deadlines at work have started slipping a little bit. I just end up staying late, trying to get comfortable enough to finally hit submit on my work. I really want to be a good employee, so I hope my boss understands I'm just trying to be thorough. 

And, um, outside of work... I guess I've kind of stopped making it to my paddleboarding meetups, and I haven't been working out as much. The checking routines just sort of... eat up the time I used to keep for myself. I tell my friends I'm just busy with work, which is kind of true, right? I just don't want them to think I'm weird or anything. 

Is that the kind of thing you're looking for? I'm sorry if I'm rambling, I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions right.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of recurrent intrusive thoughts leading to compulsive checking behaviors, significant time spent on these behaviors, and resulting impairment in social and occupational functioning strongly indicate Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). Other subtypes of OCD (F42.0, F42.1, F42.8, F42.9) are ruled out based on the predominance of checking rituals and intrusive thoughts without significant hoarding, contamination fears, or other primary obsessions.
